title: "Single and grouped brms fits"
knitr:
  opts_chunk:
    collapse: true
    comment: "#>"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
library(toxval)
```

```{r}
#| label: helpers
#| echo: false
# formatting for inline numbers, so that every value in the prose is computed
fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, digits = digits, format = "f")
pct <- function(x) paste0(formatC(100 * x, digits = 0, format = "f"), " per cent")
# one row of a toxval tibble, by direction and, for a grouped fit, by plate
pick <- function(tbl, direction, group = NULL) {
  keep <- tbl$direction == direction
  if (!is.null(group)) {
    keep <- keep & tbl$group == group
  }
  stopifnot(sum(keep) == 1)
  tbl[keep, ]
}
interval <- function(row) {
  paste0(fmt(row$estimate), " (", fmt(row$conf.low), " to ", fmt(row$conf.high), ")")
}
```

Here we apply `ecx()` and `nsec()` to a model fitted with `brm()` from the
`brms` package, first as a single curve and then with one curve for each level
of a factor. The definitions of both estimates are given in the vignettes on the
[ECx](https://open-aims.github.io/toxval/articles/ecx-definition.html) and the
[NSEC](https://open-aims.github.io/toxval/articles/nsec-definition.html).

The example is a toxicity assay repeated on replicate plates, with the plate as
the factor, and the fitted equation includes a hormesis term (an initial rise in
the response at low concentrations). The models were fitted in advance by the
script `data-raw/vignette_fits_brms.R`, and the stored fits are read below, so
that building the article requires neither Stan nor the time needed for
sampling. The software versions are given under *Provenance*.

## The plate replicate assay

The data are from the bioluminescent bacterial toxicity assay of Luter et al.
(2025), in which the whole concentration series of one experiment was run on a
single plate. The plate was repeated in four experiments with one contaminant,
and each plate is a level of the factor `plateRep`.

```{r}
#| label: load-fits
fit_single <- readRDS("fits/brms_plate_single.rds")$fit
fit_grouped <- readRDS("fits/brms_plate_grouped.rds")$fit
plates <- fit_grouped$data
head(plates[c("log_x", "plateRep", "y")])
```

```{r}
#| label: data-summary
#| echo: false
conc <- sort(unique(exp(plates$log_x)))
wells <- table(plates$plateRep, plates$log_x)
stopifnot(length(unique(c(wells))) == 1)
plate_levels <- levels(plates$plateRep)
plate_cols <- grDevices::palette.colors(length(plate_levels), "Okabe-Ito")
names(plate_cols) <- plate_levels
low_x <- min(plates$log_x)
high_x <- max(plates$log_x)
mean_low <- tapply(plates$y[plates$log_x == low_x],
                   plates$plateRep[plates$log_x == low_x], mean)
mean_high <- tapply(plates$y[plates$log_x == high_x],
                    plates$plateRep[plates$log_x == high_x], mean)
peak_at <- tapply(seq_len(nrow(plates)), plates$plateRep, function(i) {
  means <- tapply(plates$y[i], plates$log_x[i], mean)
  which.max(means)
})
# the readings equal to the largest response, and the concentrations they are at
y_max <- max(plates$y)
at_max <- plates$y == y_max
max_pos <- sort(unique(match(plates$log_x[at_max], sort(unique(plates$log_x)))))
stopifnot(
  names(which.min(mean_high)) == plate_levels[1],
  min(peak_at) > 1,
  y_max < 1,
  all(max_pos >= min(peak_at) & max_pos <= max(peak_at)),
  # each concentration is twice the one below it, the lowest included
  all(abs(diff(log2(conc)) - 1) < 0.05),
  length(conc) == 11
)
ordinal <- c("first", "second", "third", "fourth", "fifth", "sixth", "seventh")
```

The data contain `r nrow(plates)` observations (`r length(plate_levels)`
plates, each with `r wells[1, 1]` wells at each of `r length(conc)`
concentrations from `r conc[1]` to `r max(conc)`). Concentration is stored as
its natural logarithm in `log_x`, and the response `y` is a proportion on the
open interval (0, 1). Each plate held artificial seawater controls and a series
of 1:2 dilutions of the toxicant, each in four wells (Luter et al. 2025).
However, the data contain no zero concentration. The lowest concentration
(`r conc[1]`) is half the next (`r conc[2]`), the ratio between successive
dilutions. We therefore take its wells to be the controls, which were given the
concentration of one further dilution so that the logarithm is defined. Because `x_control`
defaults to the lowest concentration in the data, the control for all estimates
below is the predicted response at `r conc[1]`, which is also the start of the
prediction grid.

```{r}
#| label: fig-data
#| fig-cap: "The response of each well against concentration (log axis), coloured by plate."
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 7
op <- par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 1, 1))
plot(
  exp(plates$log_x), plates$y,
  log = "x", pch = 16, col = adjustcolor(plate_cols[plates$plateRep], 0.7),
  xlab = "Concentration", ylab = "Response"
)
legend("topright", legend = plate_levels, col = plate_cols, pch = 16, bty = "n")
par(op)
```

On each plate the response at the control was near `r fmt(mean(mean_low))`, and
it rose slightly to a peak mean at the `r ordinal[min(peak_at)]` to
`r ordinal[max(peak_at)]` concentration before declining (@fig-data). The
largest response in the data (`r fmt(y_max, 3)`) was recorded in
`r sum(at_max)` readings, at the `r paste(ordinal[max_pos], collapse = " and ")`
concentrations, i.e. within that peak. The plates differ at the highest
concentration, where the mean of plate `r plate_levels[1]` is
`r fmt(mean_high[1], 3)`, whereas the means of the other three plates are
`r fmt(min(mean_high[-1]))` to `r fmt(max(mean_high[-1]))`. The rise before the
decline is hormesis, which an equation that can only decline from the control
could not follow, so the equation fitted below includes a hormesis term.

## The model

We fitted a threshold equation with a hormesis term, written as a nonlinear
`brms` formula. Up to the threshold `nec`, the predictor is `top` plus
a linear rise in `log_x` with slope `exp(slope)`. Beyond `nec`, the difference
between that predictor and `bot` is multiplied by an exponential decay with rate
`exp(beta)`, so that the curve falls towards the lower asymptote `bot`. The
family is `Beta()`, whose default link is the logit, and the whole right-hand
side of the formula is therefore on the logit scale.

```{r}
#| label: formula
#| eval: false
library(brms)

formula_nec <- y ~ bot +
  ((top + exp(slope) * log_x) - bot) *
    exp(-exp(beta) * (log_x - nec) * step(log_x - nec))

bf_single <- bf(formula_nec, bot + top + beta + nec + slope ~ 1, nl = TRUE)
bf_grouped <- bf(formula_nec, bot + top + beta + nec + slope ~ plateRep, nl = TRUE)
```

The single fit estimates one value for each parameter, whereas the grouped fit
estimates each parameter separately for each plate (as an intercept, which is
the value for the first plate, and the difference of each other plate from it).
In the grouped fit, `plateRep` is therefore a population-level effect on each
nonlinear parameter.

We give the priors in full below. For the single fit they are centred on the
data, i.e. on a response near `r fmt(plogis(2))` (logit 2) for `top` at
`log_x = 0` (a concentration of 1, which is where `top` is defined, and not at
the control), on a lower asymptote near `r fmt(plogis(-2))` (logit -2) for
`bot`, and on a threshold inside the observed range of `log_x` for `nec`. The
grouped fit uses these priors for the intercepts, and its plate differences are
centred on 0 (no difference between plates). The intercept priors and the
difference priors are specified separately because a prior written without
`coef` applies to all coefficients of its parameter.

```{r}
#| label: priors
#| eval: false
prior_single <- c(
  prior(normal(2, 2), nlpar = "top"),
  prior(normal(-2, 2), nlpar = "bot"),
  prior(normal(1, 2), nlpar = "nec"),
  prior(normal(0, 2), nlpar = "beta"),
  prior(normal(-1, 2), nlpar = "slope")
)
prior_grouped <- c(
  prior(normal(2, 2), nlpar = "top", coef = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(-2, 2), nlpar = "bot", coef = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(1, 2), nlpar = "nec", coef = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 2), nlpar = "beta", coef = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(-1, 2), nlpar = "slope", coef = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 2), nlpar = "top"),
  prior(normal(0, 2), nlpar = "bot"),
  prior(normal(0, 1), nlpar = "nec"),
  prior(normal(0, 1), nlpar = "beta"),
  prior(normal(0, 1), nlpar = "slope")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: settings
#| echo: false
sim_single <- fit_single$fit@sim
sim_grouped <- fit_grouped$fit@sim
stopifnot(
  sim_single$chains == sim_grouped$chains,
  sim_single$iter == sim_grouped$iter,
  sim_single$warmup == sim_grouped$warmup
)
```

The precision parameter `phi` was given the `brms` default prior. Both models
were fitted with identical sampler settings: `r sim_single$chains` chains of
`r sim_single$iter` iterations (the first `r sim_single$warmup` of each used as
warmup), all parameters initialised at 0 and not at random values (`init = 0`),
draws saved for all parameters (`save_pars(all = TRUE)`), and a fixed seed.

```{r}
#| label: fit
#| eval: false
fit_single <- brm(
  bf_single, data = plates, family = Beta(), prior = prior_single,
  chains = 4, iter = 5000, warmup = 2500, init = 0,
  save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE), seed = 700
)
fit_grouped <- brm(
  bf_grouped, data = plates, family = Beta(), prior = prior_grouped,
  chains = 4, iter = 5000, warmup = 2500, init = 0,
  save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE), seed = 700
)
```

The stored fits were made by `data-raw/vignette_fits_brms.R` with these
arguments, with the four chains run in parallel and no warmup draws kept.

```{r}
#| label: convergence
#| echo: false
diagnostics <- function(fit) {
  np <- brms::nuts_params(fit)
  c(
    draws = brms::ndraws(fit),
    divergent = sum(np$Value[np$Parameter == "divergent__"]),
    rhat = max(brms::rhat(fit), na.rm = TRUE),
    ess = min(brms::neff_ratio(fit), na.rm = TRUE) * brms::ndraws(fit)
  )
}
diag_single <- diagnostics(fit_single)
diag_grouped <- diagnostics(fit_grouped)
stopifnot(
  diag_single["draws"] == diag_grouped["draws"],
  fit_single$fit@sim$thin == 1, fit_grouped$fit@sim$thin == 1,
  diag_single["divergent"] == 0, diag_grouped["divergent"] == 0,
  diag_single["rhat"] < 1.01, diag_grouped["rhat"] < 1.01
)
```

Each fit contains `r format(diag_single[["draws"]], big.mark = ",")` posterior
draws, without thinning, and no divergent transitions occurred in either fit.
The largest R-hat is `r fmt(diag_single["rhat"], 3)` for the single fit and
`r fmt(diag_grouped["rhat"], 3)` for the grouped fit, and the smallest effective
sample sizes (calculated from `neff_ratio()`) are `r round(diag_single["ess"])`
and `r round(diag_grouped["ess"])` draws, respectively.

## Estimates from the single fit

A `brmsfit` may have several predictors, and in a nonlinear formula these are
mixed with the parameters, so the user must name the predictor with `x_var`. If
`x_var` is not given, the call is refused:

```{r}
#| label: no-x-var
#| error: true
ecx(fit_single)
```

Because the model was fitted on log concentration, we use `xform = exp` to
return each estimate as a concentration. The transformation is applied to each
realisation before summarising, so that the median and the interval limits are
those of the concentrations. The argument `xform` is optional, and without it
the estimates are returned on the `log_x` scale.

```{r}
#| label: single-ecx
ecx_single <- ecx(fit_single, x_var = "log_x", xform = exp)
ecx_single
```

```{r}
#| label: single-nsec
nsec_single <- nsec(fit_single, x_var = "log_x", xform = exp)
nsec_single
```

Every argument of this call other than `x_var` and `xform` takes its default.
@tbl-nsec-columns gives the value of each column of the decreasing row, what it
is, and the argument and default that set it. The `ecx()` result has the same
columns, with `proportion` in place of `sig_val` and without `anchor` and
`ecnsec`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-nsec-columns
#| tbl-cap: "The columns of the decreasing row of `nsec_single`, and the setting (the toxval default in each case) from which each value follows."
#| echo: false
nsec_s_dec <- pick(nsec_single, "decreasing")
nsec_s_inc <- pick(nsec_single, "increasing")
x_steps <- diff(toxval_predict(fit_single, x_var = "log_x")$x_vec)
stopifnot(
  nsec_s_dec$sig_val == 0.01, nsec_s_dec$type == "absolute",
  nsec_s_dec$anchor == "model", is.na(nsec_s_dec$asymptote),
  length(x_steps) == 499, diff(range(x_steps)) < 1e-8
)
columns <- data.frame(
  Column = c(
    "`metric`, `direction`", "`estimate`, `conf.low`, `conf.high`",
    "`sig_val`", "`control`", "`reference`", "`type`",
    "`ecnsec`, `ecnsec.low`, `ecnsec.high`", "`asymptote`", "`anchor`",
    "`resolution` (in the header)"
  ),
  Value = c(
    "nsec, decreasing", interval(nsec_s_dec), fmt(nsec_s_dec$sig_val),
    fmt(nsec_s_dec$control, 3), fmt(nsec_s_dec$reference, 3),
    nsec_s_dec$type,
    paste0(pct(nsec_s_dec$ecnsec), " (", pct(nsec_s_dec$ecnsec.low), " to ",
           pct(nsec_s_dec$ecnsec.high), ")"),
    "NA", nsec_s_dec$anchor, "500"
  ),
  Meaning = c(
    "The estimate and the direction of the change. Both directions are always returned.",
    "The median and 95 per cent interval of the NSEC realisations, after `xform`.",
    "The quantile of the control realisations that sets the decreasing reference; 1 - `sig_val` sets the increasing one.",
    paste0("The median predicted response at the control concentration (", round(conc[1], 2), ")."),
    "The `sig_val` quantile of the control realisations. The NSEC is the first concentration at which the curve falls below it.",
    "The span that `ecnsec` is a proportion of: for a decreasing response under `\"absolute\"`, from the control to 0.",
    "The decline at the NSEC as a proportion of that span, i.e. of the control here.",
    "The asymptote that `ecnsec` is measured to under `type = \"relative\"`; `NA` otherwise.",
    "The control the reference is taken from in a model-averaged fit. A `brmsfit` is one model, so it has no effect here.",
    paste0("The number of concentrations, evenly spaced on the `log_x` scale from ",
           round(conc[1], 2), " to ", max(conc), ", at which each realisation is evaluated.")
  ),
  `Set by` = c(
    "", "`prob_vals = c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975)`", "`sig_val = 0.01`",
    "`x_control = NULL`: the lowest concentration in the data",
    "`sig_val`", "`type = \"absolute\"`", "`type`, `prob_vals`", "`type`",
    "`anchor = NULL`: `\"model\"`, except `\"component\"` for a `bayesmanecfit`",
    "`resolution = 500`; `x_range = NULL`: the range of the data"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(columns)
```

The `anchor` argument changes the result only for a model-averaged fit, and is
shown on one in the
[`bayesnec` case study](https://open-aims.github.io/toxval/articles/case-bayesnec.html#the-nsec-reference-under-model-averaging).

To show these estimates against the fitted curve, we predicted the curve with
`toxval_predict()`. Called with the same `x_var`, it gives the curve from which
`ecx()` and `nsec()` obtained the estimates above: a matrix of predicted
responses, with one row for each posterior draw and one column for each value of
the grid `x_vec` (on the `log_x` scale). We use two functions for this figure
and for the figure of the plates. `marks_of()` collects the
rows of an `ecx()` and an `nsec()` result, and `plot_fit()` draws the data, the
posterior median curve with its 95 per cent credible band, each estimate with
its interval, and the reference of each NSEC.

```{r}
#| label: plot-helpers
est_cols <- c(
  "EC10 decreasing" = "#0072B2", "NSEC decreasing" = "#D55E00",
  "EC10 increasing" = "#CC79A7", "NSEC increasing" = "#E69F00"
)

marks_of <- function(ecx_tbl, nsec_tbl, level = NULL) {
  rows <- function(tbl) if (is.null(level)) tbl else tbl[tbl$group == level, ]
  cols <- c("direction", "estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high", "reference")
  rbind(
    data.frame(metric = "EC10", rows(ecx_tbl)[cols]),
    data.frame(metric = "NSEC", rows(nsec_tbl)[cols])
  )
}

plot_fit <- function(x_vec, curve, x, y, marks, main = NULL) {
  q <- apply(curve, 2, quantile, c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975))
  plot(x, y, log = "x", ylim = c(0, 1), pch = 16,
       col = adjustcolor("grey60", 0.7), xlab = "Concentration",
       ylab = "Response", main = main, cex.main = 0.95, font.main = 1)
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(marks))) {
    col <- est_cols[[paste(marks$metric[i], marks$direction[i])]]
    lim <- c(marks$conf.low[i], marks$conf.high[i])
    # An interval that reaches the highest concentration is censored there,
    # so draw its limits as dashed lines rather than a band.
    if (lim[2] >= max(x)) {
      abline(v = lim, col = col, lty = 2)
    } else {
      rect(lim[1], -1, lim[2], 2, col = adjustcolor(col, 0.15), border = NA)
    }
    abline(v = marks$estimate[i], col = col, lwd = 2)
    if (marks$metric[i] == "NSEC") {
      abline(h = marks$reference[i], col = col, lty = 3)
    }
  }
  polygon(exp(c(x_vec, rev(x_vec))), c(q[2, ], rev(q[3, ])),
          col = adjustcolor("black", 0.2), border = NA)
  lines(exp(x_vec), q[1, ], lwd = 2)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-single
#| fig-cap: "The single fit. The data of all four plates (grey points), the posterior median curve (black line) and its 95 per cent credible band (grey), with the median of each estimate (vertical lines). The 95 per cent interval of an estimate is shaded in its colour, or marked by dashed lines where its upper limit is the highest concentration. The reference of each NSEC is a dotted horizontal line in its colour. The concentration axis is logarithmic."
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 7
pred_single <- toxval_predict(fit_single, x_var = "log_x")

op <- par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 1, 1))
plot_fit(pred_single$x_vec, pred_single$curves[[1]],
         exp(plates$log_x), plates$y, marks_of(ecx_single, nsec_single))
legend(8, 0.8, legend = names(est_cols), col = est_cols, lwd = 2,
       bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
par(op)
```

```{r}
#| label: single-read
#| echo: false
ecx_s_dec <- pick(ecx_single, "decreasing")
ecx_s_inc <- pick(ecx_single, "increasing")
band <-function(curve) apply(curve, 2, quantile, c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975))
peak_x <- function(x_vec, curve) exp(x_vec[which.max(band(curve)[1, ])])
peak_single <- peak_x(pred_single$x_vec, pred_single$curves[[1]])
stopifnot(
  ecx_s_inc$conf.high == max(conc),
  ecx_s_inc$estimate < ecx_s_dec$conf.low,
  # nearest test concentration, on the log scale, is the second
  which.min(abs(log(conc) - log(ecx_s_inc$estimate))) == 2,
  nsec_s_dec$estimate < ecx_s_dec$estimate,
  nsec_s_dec$ecnsec < 0.1,
  nsec_s_inc$conf.high == max(conc),
  ecx_s_inc$estimate < peak_single, nsec_s_inc$estimate < peak_single,
  ecx_s_dec$estimate > peak_single, nsec_s_dec$estimate > peak_single
)
```

The median curve of the single fit peaks at a concentration of
`r fmt(peak_single)` (@fig-single). In the decreasing direction the EC10 is
`r interval(ecx_s_dec)` (blue), i.e. the concentration on the decline at which
the curve falls from the control (`r fmt(ecx_s_dec$control, 3)`) to
`r fmt(ecx_s_dec$reference, 3)` (10 per cent of the way from the control to 0).
The decreasing NSEC is `r interval(nsec_s_dec)` (vermillion), which is below the
EC10 because its reference (`r fmt(nsec_s_dec$reference, 3)`, the dotted
vermillion line) is closer to the control than the EC10 reference. At the NSEC
the decline is `r pct(nsec_s_dec$ecnsec)` of the control (@tbl-nsec-columns).

For each realisation, `ecx()` and `nsec()` take the first concentration at which
the curve crosses the reference in the direction of the row, interpolated
between grid points. Because the curve first rises above the control, the
decreasing references are crossed only on the decline beyond the peak, and the
increasing references only on the rise below it. Under `type = "absolute"` a
Beta response is a proportion, so the increasing reference of the EC10 is the
control plus 10 per cent of the difference between the control and 1
(`r fmt(ecx_s_inc$reference, 3)`). The increasing EC10 is
`r fmt(ecx_s_inc$estimate, 3)` (pink), close to the second concentration
(`r conc[2]`), and the increasing NSEC, at which the rise exceeds the 0.99
quantile of the control (`r fmt(nsec_s_inc$reference, 3)`, the dotted orange
line), is `r fmt(nsec_s_inc$estimate)` (orange). In some realisations the
response never rises as far as these references, and the upper limit of both
intervals is therefore the highest concentration (`r max(conc)`, dashed lines),
as the warnings report. How toxval places such realisations is shown in the
[multivariate `brms` case study](https://open-aims.github.io/toxval/articles/case-brms-multivariate.html).

## Estimates for each plate

With `group_var = "plateRep"`, one curve is predicted, and one estimate
returned, for each plate. This requires `plateRep` to be a population-level
effect in the fit (as it is here), because `toxval_predict()` marginalises over
group-level effects. A plate entered only as `(1 | plateRep)` would give all
plates one common curve, and the call would be refused.

```{r}
#| label: grouped-ecx
ecx_grouped <- ecx(fit_grouped, x_var = "log_x", group_var = "plateRep", xform = exp)
ecx_grouped[, c("direction", "group", "estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high", "control")]
```

```{r}
#| label: grouped-nsec
nsec_grouped <- nsec(
  fit_grouped,
  x_var = "log_x", group_var = "plateRep", xform = exp, draws = TRUE
)
nsec_grouped[, c("direction", "group", "estimate", "control", "reference", "ecnsec")]
```

```{r}
#| label: grouped-controls
#| echo: false
dec_nsec <- nsec_grouped[nsec_grouped$direction == "decreasing", ]
inc_nsec <- nsec_grouped[nsec_grouped$direction == "increasing", ]
stopifnot(
  identical(dec_nsec$control, inc_nsec$control),
  all(dec_nsec$reference < dec_nsec$control),
  all(inc_nsec$reference > inc_nsec$control),
  length(unique(dec_nsec$reference)) == length(plate_levels)
)
```

Each plate has its own `control`, predicted from that plate's curve at
`r conc[1]`, and its own `reference`, the 0.01 (decreasing) or 0.99
(increasing) quantile of that plate's control realisations. The NSEC of each
plate is therefore measured against the variation of its own control. The
controls range from `r fmt(min(dec_nsec$control), 3)` to
`r fmt(max(dec_nsec$control), 3)`, and the decreasing references from
`r fmt(min(dec_nsec$reference), 3)` to `r fmt(max(dec_nsec$reference), 3)`.

For the grouped fit, `toxval_predict()` returns one curve for each plate in
`curves`, and the plate of each curve is given in `keys$group`. Below we draw
each plate with its own curve and estimates, using the functions defined above.

```{r}
#| label: fig-plates
#| fig-cap: "The grouped fit, one panel for each plate. Each panel shows the data of that plate (grey points), its posterior median curve (black line) and 95 per cent credible band (grey), and the median and 95 per cent interval of each of its estimates, as in @fig-single. The concentration axis is logarithmic."
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-width: 8
pred_grouped <- toxval_predict(fit_grouped, x_var = "log_x", group_var = "plateRep")

op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 2, 0.8))
for (i in seq_along(pred_grouped$curves)) {
  level <- as.character(pred_grouped$keys$group[i])
  in_plate <- plates$plateRep == level
  plot_fit(pred_grouped$x_vec, pred_grouped$curves[[i]],
           exp(plates$log_x[in_plate]), plates$y[in_plate],
           marks_of(ecx_grouped, nsec_grouped, level), main = level)
  if (i == 1) {
    legend(90, 0.8, xjust = 1, legend = names(est_cols), col = est_cols, lwd = 2,
           bty = "n", cex = 0.75)
  }
}
par(op)
```

```{r}
#| label: grouped-read
#| echo: false
dec_ecx <- ecx_grouped[ecx_grouped$direction == "decreasing", ]
dec_nsec <- nsec_grouped[nsec_grouped$direction == "decreasing", ]
inc_nsec <- nsec_grouped[nsec_grouped$direction == "increasing", ]
inc_ecx <- ecx_grouped[ecx_grouped$direction == "increasing", ]
curve_of <- function(level) {
  pred_grouped$curves[[match(level, as.character(pred_grouped$keys$group))]]
}
end_single <- band(pred_single$curves[[1]])[, length(pred_single$x_vec)]
end_grouped <- vapply(plate_levels, function(level) {
  stats::median(curve_of(level)[, length(pred_grouped$x_vec)])
}, numeric(1))
peak_plates <- vapply(plate_levels, function(level) {
  peak_x(pred_grouped$x_vec, curve_of(level))
}, numeric(1))
by_plate <- function(tbl) tbl$estimate[match(plate_levels, tbl$group)]
inc_ecx_inside <- as.character(inc_ecx$group[inc_ecx$conf.high < max(conc)])
stopifnot(
  identical(as.character(dec_nsec$group), plate_levels),
  which.min(dec_nsec$estimate) == 1,
  identical(order(dec_ecx$estimate), order(dec_nsec$estimate)),
  dec_nsec$conf.high[1] < min(dec_nsec$conf.low[-1]),
  all(inc_nsec$conf.high == max(conc)),
  all(dec_nsec$estimate < dec_ecx$estimate),
  names(which.min(end_grouped)) == plate_levels[1],
  end_single[1] > min(mean_high), end_single[1] < max(mean_high),
  all(by_plate(inc_ecx) < peak_plates), all(by_plate(inc_nsec) < peak_plates),
  all(by_plate(dec_nsec) > peak_plates),
  identical(inc_ecx_inside, plate_levels[1:2])
)
```

For plate `r plate_levels[1]` the decreasing NSEC is
`r interval(dec_nsec[1, ])`, and its interval is below the intervals of the
other three plates, whose estimates are `r fmt(min(dec_nsec$estimate[-1]))` to
`r fmt(max(dec_nsec$estimate[-1]))` (@fig-plates). This is the plate whose
response falls furthest. At the highest concentration its median curve is
`r fmt(end_grouped[1], 3)` (against an observed mean of
`r fmt(mean_high[1], 3)`), whereas the median curves of the other three plates
are `r fmt(min(end_grouped[-1]))` to `r fmt(max(end_grouped[-1]))`. The
decreasing EC10 estimates order the plates identically, from
`r fmt(dec_ecx$estimate[1])` for plate `r plate_levels[1]` to
`r fmt(max(dec_ecx$estimate))`. At the decreasing NSEC of each plate, the
decline (`ecnsec`) is `r pct(min(dec_nsec$ecnsec))` to
`r pct(max(dec_nsec$ecnsec))` of its control. Together with the narrow range
of the controls, this suggests that the plates differ in where the decline
begins and how far it goes, and not in their response at the control.

The median curves of the plates peak at concentrations of
`r fmt(min(peak_plates))` to `r fmt(max(peak_plates))`. As for the single fit,
the increasing estimates of each plate are on the rise below that peak and the
decreasing estimates on the decline above it. The intervals of the increasing
estimates extend to the highest concentration, with the exception of the
increasing EC10 of plates `r inc_ecx_inside[1]` and `r inc_ecx_inside[2]`. By
contrast, the single fit gives one curve for all four plates, and at the highest
concentration its median is `r fmt(end_single[1], 3)` (with a credible band of
`r fmt(end_single[2], 3)` to `r fmt(end_single[3], 3)`), which is between the
plate means of `r fmt(min(mean_high), 3)` to `r fmt(max(mean_high), 3)`
(@fig-single).

Without `group_var`, predictions cannot be made from the grouped fit, because
each prediction requires a plate:

```{r}
#| label: grouped-no-group-var
#| error: true
nsec(fit_grouped, x_var = "log_x")
```

## Pooling the plates

The toxval package does not pool estimates across the levels of a
population-level effect. However, the user can pool the decreasing NSEC
realisations of the plates (returned with `draws = TRUE`) to obtain one value
across plates:

```{r}
#| label: pooled
pooled <- unlist(lapply(dec_nsec$draws, function(d) d$value.draw))
pooled_q <- quantile(pooled, c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975))
pooled_q
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pooled
#| fig-cap: "The data of all four plates (grey points) and the posterior median curve of each plate from the grouped fit (black, one line type per plate), with the decreasing NSEC of each plate (open circles, on its curve). The median of the pooled decreasing NSEC is marked by the vermillion line, and its 95 per cent interval by the vermillion band. The concentration axis is logarithmic."
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 7
nsec_col <- est_cols[["NSEC decreasing"]]
op <- par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 1, 1))
plot(exp(plates$log_x), plates$y, log = "x", ylim = c(0, 1), pch = 16,
     col = adjustcolor("grey60", 0.7), xlab = "Concentration", ylab = "Response")
rect(pooled_q[2], -1, pooled_q[3], 2, col = adjustcolor(nsec_col, 0.15), border = NA)
abline(v = pooled_q[1], col = nsec_col, lwd = 2)
for (i in seq_along(pred_grouped$curves)) {
  median_curve <- apply(pred_grouped$curves[[i]], 2, median)
  lines(exp(pred_grouped$x_vec), median_curve, lty = i, lwd = 2)
  level <- as.character(pred_grouped$keys$group[i])
  at <- dec_nsec$estimate[dec_nsec$group == level]
  points(at, approx(exp(pred_grouped$x_vec), median_curve, at)$y, cex = 1.3, lwd = 2)
}
legend("topright", bty = "n", cex = 0.8, lwd = 2,
       legend = c(as.character(pred_grouped$keys$group), "Pooled NSEC, decreasing"),
       lty = c(seq_along(pred_grouped$curves), 1),
       col = c(rep("black", length(pred_grouped$curves)), nsec_col))
par(op)
```

```{r}
#| label: pooled-read
#| echo: false
stopifnot(
  all(is.finite(pooled)),
  diff(pooled_q[2:3]) > max(dec_nsec$conf.high - dec_nsec$conf.low),
  pooled_q[2] < min(dec_nsec$estimate), pooled_q[3] > max(dec_nsec$estimate)
)
```

The pooled decreasing NSEC is `r fmt(pooled_q[1])` (`r fmt(pooled_q[2])` to
`r fmt(pooled_q[3])`). Its interval includes the decreasing NSEC of each plate
(`r fmt(min(dec_nsec$estimate))` to `r fmt(max(dec_nsec$estimate))`, the open
circles in @fig-pooled), and it is wider than the interval of any individual
plate, because it includes the difference between plates.

## The `nec` parameter and the NSEC

The `nec` parameter of the equation is a threshold within the equation, and is
not a toxicity estimate computed from the fitted curve. The toxval package
computes estimates from the fitted curve only, so we take the `nec` parameter
from the posterior draws of each fit with `as_draws_df()`. The parameter is on
the `log_x` scale. In the grouped fit, `b_nec_Intercept` is the value for the
first plate, and the value for each other plate is the intercept plus the
difference for that plate.

```{r}
#| label: nec-parameter
nec_single <- exp(brms::as_draws_df(fit_single, variable = "b_nec_Intercept")$b_nec_Intercept)

draws_grouped <- brms::as_draws_df(fit_grouped, variable = "^b_nec_", regex = TRUE)
nec_grouped <- sapply(plate_levels, function(level) {
  log_nec <- draws_grouped$b_nec_Intercept
  difference <- paste0("b_nec_plateRep", level)
  if (difference %in% names(draws_grouped)) {
    log_nec <- log_nec + draws_grouped[[difference]]
  }
  exp(log_nec)
})
apply(nec_grouped, 2, quantile, c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975))
```

```{r}
#| label: nec-parameter-read
#| echo: false
nec_check <- exp(brms::posterior_epred(
  fit_grouped, newdata = data.frame(log_x = 0, plateRep = plate_levels), nlpar = "nec"
))
nec_s_q <- quantile(nec_single, c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975))
nec_g_q <- apply(nec_grouped, 2, quantile, c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975))
nec_pool_q <- quantile(c(nec_grouped), c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975))
stopifnot(
  length(nec_single) == diag_single[["draws"]],
  isTRUE(all.equal(unname(nec_grouped), unname(nec_check))),
  nec_s_q[1] < nsec_s_dec$estimate,
  all(nec_g_q[1, ] < dec_nsec$estimate),
  nec_pool_q[1] < pooled_q[1]
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-nec
#| fig-cap: "The median and 95 per cent interval of the `nec` parameter (grey) and of the decreasing NSEC (vermillion), for the single fit, for each plate of the grouped fit, and for the realisations of the four plates pooled. The concentration axis is logarithmic."
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-width: 7
nec_rows <- rbind("Single fit" = nec_s_q, t(nec_g_q), "Plates pooled" = nec_pool_q)
nsec_rows <- rbind(
  unlist(nsec_s_dec[c("estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high")]),
  as.matrix(dec_nsec[match(plate_levels, dec_nsec$group),
                     c("estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high")]),
  pooled_q
)
at <- rev(seq_len(nrow(nec_rows)))
op <- par(mar = c(4.5, 11, 1, 1))
plot(NA, log = "x", xlim = range(nec_rows, nsec_rows), ylim = c(0.5, max(at) + 1),
     yaxt = "n", xlab = "Concentration", ylab = "")
axis(2, at = at, labels = rownames(nec_rows), las = 1, cex.axis = 0.8)
segments(nec_rows[, 2], at + 0.12, nec_rows[, 3], at + 0.12, col = "grey40", lwd = 2)
points(nec_rows[, 1], at + 0.12, pch = 16, col = "grey40")
segments(nsec_rows[, 2], at - 0.12, nsec_rows[, 3], at - 0.12, col = nsec_col, lwd = 2)
points(nsec_rows[, 1], at - 0.12, pch = 16, col = nsec_col)
legend("top", horiz = TRUE, bty = "n", cex = 0.8, pch = 16, lwd = 2,
       col = c("grey40", nsec_col), legend = c("nec parameter", "NSEC, decreasing"))
par(op)
```

For the single fit the `nec` parameter is `r fmt(nec_s_q[1])`
(`r fmt(nec_s_q[2])` to `r fmt(nec_s_q[3])`), compared with a decreasing NSEC of
`r fmt(nsec_s_dec$estimate)`. For the grouped fit it is
`r fmt(min(nec_g_q[1, ]))` to `r fmt(max(nec_g_q[1, ]))` across the plates, and
`r fmt(nec_pool_q[1])` (`r fmt(nec_pool_q[2])` to `r fmt(nec_pool_q[3])`) when
the realisations of the plates are pooled as for the NSEC above. In each fit the
median of the `nec` parameter is below the decreasing NSEC (@fig-nec). This is
because the parameter marks where the hormetic rise ends and the decay begins,
after which the response must fall back past the control and below the 0.01
quantile of the control realisations, which occurs only at a higher
concentration.

## Provenance

```{r}
#| label: provenance
#| echo: false
prov_single <- readRDS("fits/brms_plate_single.rds")$provenance
prov_grouped <- readRDS("fits/brms_plate_grouped.rds")$provenance
size_mb <- function(file) fmt(file.size(file) / 1e6)
# The commit is that of the checkout the article is rendered from. The site
# build installs toxval from the same checkout.
toxval_commit <- tryCatch(
  system2("git", c("rev-parse", "HEAD"), stdout = TRUE, stderr = FALSE),
  error = function(e) "not recorded",
  warning = function(w) "not recorded"
)
```

- Data: `data-raw/example_pgl.csv`, from the assay of Luter et al. (2025). The
  first, unnamed column of the file is a row index and is dropped.
- Fits: made by `data-raw/vignette_fits_brms.R` with seed
  `r prov_single$seed`, on `r format(prov_single$fitted_on, "%Y-%m-%d")`, with
  `r prov_single$r_version`, `brms` `r prov_single$packages[["brms"]]` and
  `rstan` `r prov_single$packages[["rstan"]]`. Fitting, including compilation
  of the Stan program, took `r round(prov_single$fit_seconds)` s for the single
  fit and `r round(prov_grouped$fit_seconds)` s for the grouped fit. The stored
  files are `r size_mb("fits/brms_plate_single.rds")` MB and
  `r size_mb("fits/brms_plate_grouped.rds")` MB. Each keeps all
  `r format(diag_single[["draws"]], big.mark = ",")` post-warmup draws; warmup
  draws and the compiled Stan program are not stored.
- Rendered with toxval `r utils::packageVersion("toxval")` at commit
  `r toxval_commit`, `brms`
  `r utils::packageVersion("brms")` and `r R.version.string`.

Luter, H. M., Damjanovic, K., Thomas, M. C., Fisher, R., Høj, L. and Negri,
A. P. (2025). A bioluminescent bacterial toxicity assay for tropical marine
environments. *Environmental Toxicology*.
<https://doi.org/10.1002/tox.70003>
